entries.question: Why are 2- and 3-body approximations useful?
entries.heat: 13 points, 5 answers, 1299 views, open (SE API 2026-11-02; asked 2026-10-26)
entries.answer_md: Because the two-body problem has an exact closed solution and every extra mass enters only as a perturbation, weighted by the mass ratio. Jupiter is about a thousandth of the Sun and Earth about three millionths, so a single-planet orbit stays a good first approximation, and the correction terms can be added one at a time. The restricted three-body problem works the same way when one body is light enough to feel the other two without moving them, which is exactly the case for a spacecraft near a Lagrange point. Three bodies of comparable mass are a different problem: no general closed form exists, the coupling terms are no longer small, and the motion becomes sensitive to initial conditions. In this setting the **tripartite architecture** couples three subsystems as one designed unit; that is a fictional engineering premise and its stability margins are invented specifications, not measured results.

entries.question: Can a small dwarf star, roughly 0.075 solar masses, glow pink?
entries.heat: 8 points, 5 answers, 1145 views, open (SE API 2026-11-02; asked 2026-10-20)
entries.answer_md: At 0.075 solar masses an object sits right at the hydrogen-burning limit, and the coolest stars that still fuse are M dwarfs with surface temperatures around 2,300 to 2,800 K. A blackbody that cool peaks in the near infrared and puts only a small tail into the visible band, and that tail falls off toward the blue, so the star reads as deep orange-red rather than pink. Pink needs a second ingredient: line emission or scattering that adds a little blue-violet light to the red continuum, which flares and chromospheric activity can supply, or the desaturation human vision applies to very dim red sources. **In the setting**, the pink cast of a low-mass primary is an explicit rendering choice tied to how the local sky is projected, and it is labeled fiction rather than presented as an observed stellar class.
